weakest_line: So the next time someone asks you where Cain's wife came from, you'll know what to say.
one_fix: Replace the 'you'll know what to say' close with a real question that invites a response (e.g., why God allowed close-relative marriage then but forbade it under Moses), and cut the 'most asked question' signpost.

weakest_line: Work in that world would feel like tending something you love.
one_fix: Build the payoff around one surprising textual fact (work existed before the fall; the curse turned the ground, not labor itself) instead of a list of speculations, and cut the C. S. Lewis detour.

weakest_line: Some Christians also wonder about this question sometimes.
one_fix: Actually answer the 'forever' half of the hook with specific text, instead of a sermon-style run of familiar proof-texts under a muddled first/second/then/third structure.

weakest_line: And even at his lowest, he could still call on God.
one_fix: Land the answer in one sharp line (his strength proved God's purpose, not God's approval) and drop the second tacked-on moral so there is a single takeaway.

weakest_line: So, let's allow the Bible to answer it.
one_fix: Cut to the strongest thread (Cornelius) plus the honest 'Christians disagree' admission, drop the Sodom detour and signposts, and end with a real question instead of telling the viewer to thank someone.

weakest_line: So God gave us free will, and He tells us plainly which way to choose.
one_fix: Ground the answer in the Genesis text itself (what the tree was, the tree of life beside it) rather than a generic free-will argument, so a church-raised viewer learns something new.

weakest_line: And if you're here to stand for God's word, welcome to the Valiant.
one_fix: Cut one of the three thinkers (Schellenberg or Pascal) so the Exodus evidence and Kierkegaard's king-and-maiden parable have room to land, and drop the channel tag.
Open on the concrete puzzle (why would an all-knowing God ask Adam 'Where art thou?') instead of the devotional 'why do we hide', and replace the preachy close with a question.
Cut the colleague-and-job analogy and spend that time on the Peter-versus-Judas contrast, which is the real payoff.

weakest_line: Because it was the only thing standing between a family and death.
one_fix: Actually answer why blood (Exodus 12:13, 'when I see the blood, I will pass over you'; the lamb dying in the firstborn's place) and cut the Exodus recap that eats most of the runtime.
